prompt.context: It is May 1, 2015. Your client is Nick Tupoi, who recently accepted his offer to join Fuqua's class of 2017. He is from Eastern Europe and currently owns a startup there.
prompt.question: Nick is looking for your advice on what to do with the company once he leaves for Durham.

clarifying_info.a: The company's business is in the outdoor advertising space. The company owns 8 advertising billboards in a major Eastern European city and rents them out.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the company been operating?
clarifying_info.a: Nick started the company 2 years ago and it has been profitable since then.

clarifying_info.q: How many employees does the company have?
clarifying_info.a: The company has no full-time employees except for Nick himself. Short-term contractors are hired from time to time.

clarifying_info.q: What are Nick's plans after his MBA?
clarifying_info.a: Nick wants to stay and work in the US after his MBA.
Nick owns 80% of the company; the other 20% is owned by his partner.

clarifying_info.q: Does Nick do most of the work?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Nick does most of the work — everything from generating sales to maintaining the billboards.

clarifying_info.q: Does Nick have savings to cover tuition?
clarifying_info.a: Nick does not have enough savings to cover tuition at Duke. He has taken a loan to finance his MBA.

clarifying_info.q: Can Nick's partner run the business?
clarifying_info.a: His partner has a full-time job and is not interested in running the company.

clarifying_info.q: What is the occupancy rate of the billboards?
clarifying_info.a: All 8 billboards are rented out for the whole year — 100% occupancy.

clarifying_info.q: How long are the typical contracts?
Are all billboards the same size and price?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the size and price are the same for all 8 billboards — see Exhibit 1.
All the costs are covered by the first month's revenue from the contracts. Ignore all other costs including depreciation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the income tax rate?
What discount rate should I use?
clarifying_info.a: Nick does not know what discount rate would be appropriate. He is a Fuqua student and can take a student loan at 8.5% interest. He wants you to determine an appropriate discount rate.

exhibits.title: Billboard Size and Pricing
exhibits.shows: A table showing the size and monthly rental price of the billboards. Note: price displayed is monthly rent.
exhibits.data: Billboard size: 500 sq ft (25 x 20 ft); Renting price: $5,500/month; Sales tax: $1/sq ft

framework: Assess two main strategic options: (1) run the business remotely while doing the MBA, or (2) sell the business
Evaluate Option 1 (remote operation): analyze feasibility given Nick's sole-employee status, customer relationship management challenges, and financial needs
Evaluate Option 2 (sale): identify potential buyers, value the business, and determine an appropriate asking price
Recommend a course of action and flag key risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Should Nick try to run the business remotely while completing his MBA?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate concludes this is NOT a viable option. Key reasons: (1) Nick is the sole employee and runs everything himself — finding and funding a replacement in time is impractical; (2) managing customer relationships from afar over the phone is difficult for a business built on personal selling; (3) Nick lacks the savings to cover tuition and has taken a student loan, meaning he needs the cash from the business now, not an ongoing income stream that might be disrupted.

questions.prompt: Who are the potential buyers for Nick's business?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm multiple buyer categories: (1) Nick's existing business partner; (2) direct competitors in outdoor advertising; (3) the company's major clients who might want to own the assets; (4) private equity or local investors looking for stable yield assets; (5) media or marketing agencies. The partner is the most obvious but has already declined to run the business, and his interest in acquiring equity is uncertain.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate discount rate to use in valuing the business, and why?
questions.guidance: There is no single correct answer — the question tests independent judgment under ambiguity. The 8.5% student loan rate is a deliberate anchor and should be questioned: it reflects Nick's personal borrowing cost, not the risk of the business. Factors pulling toward a LOWER rate: the business is mature, asset-driven, has 100% occupancy, and has been consistently profitable since inception (low operational risk). Factors pulling toward a HIGHER rate: the business depends entirely on Nick and may be worth much less to an outside operator (key-man risk); Nick needs to sell quickly, so the buyer will price in a liquidity discount. A reasonable range is 15%–30%; a strong candidate picks a rate and justifies it rather than hedging indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV (valuation) of the business using a perpetuity model and determine Nick's share of the proceeds.
questions.guidance: Walk through revenue per billboard, apply sales tax, compute net revenue, scale to all 8 billboards, subtract costs (= 1 month's revenue per 6-month contract), apply 20% income tax, then divide net income by the chosen discount rate. After getting the NPV, candidates should note that the company is worth significantly more than the cost of Nick's MBA, and that a fire-sale timeline will depress the valuation — suggesting Nick might explore alternatives such as a structured sale over a longer horizon or a partial buyout by the partner.

math.setup: Perpetuity valuation: NPV = Net Income / Discount Rate; Net Income = (Total Revenue - Total Costs) x (1 - Tax Rate); Costs = 1 month of revenue per 6-month contract cycle
steps: Net revenue per billboard per month = $5,500 - $500 = $5,000
Net revenue per billboard per year = $5,000 x 12 = $60,000
Total annual costs = $480,000 / 6 = $80,000 (costs = 1 month of revenue per 6-month contract)
Nick's 80% share at 25% discount rate = $1,280,000 x 0.80 = $1,024,000
math.answer: At a 25% discount rate, the business is worth approximately $1,280,000 in total; Nick's 80% share is ~$1,024,000. The valuation is highly sensitive to the discount rate chosen (ranges from ~$640K to ~$3.2M across 50%–10%).

brainstorming.prompt: Who are the potential buyers Nick could sell his billboard business to?

categories.name: Insiders
ideas: Key employees or contractors who know the business

categories.name: Competitors
ideas: Other outdoor advertising companies in the city
National or regional billboard operators looking to expand

categories.name: Clients
ideas: Advertisers who are current tenants and want to control their inventory
Local businesses that are frequent repeat clients

categories.name: Financial buyers
ideas: Local private equity or family offices seeking stable yield
Individual investors looking for a cash-flow asset

categories.name: Strategic buyers
ideas: Media agencies wanting physical advertising assets
Marketing conglomerates expanding into Eastern Europe

recommendation: Nick should sell the business rather than attempt to run it remotely; the key-man dependency, customer relationship requirements, and his financial need for tuition cash all make remote operation impractical

The business should be valued using a discount rate in the 15%–25% range, yielding a total enterprise value of approximately $1.3M–$2.1M and a ~$1.0M–$1.7M payout for Nick's 80% stake — well above his MBA tuition cost
risks: Selling quickly will compress valuation; a buyer will demand a liquidity discount for a fast close
The business loses significant value without Nick, making it harder to command a premium price
The partner's stake (20%) may complicate negotiations if he disagrees on price or buyer
next_steps: Approach the partner first — a buyout or facilitated sale keeps the process simple
Simultaneously engage 2–3 competitor or client buyers to create competitive tension and improve price
Consider whether Nick can structure a short earn-out or transition period (1–3 months) to train a replacement and protect valuation
An excellent candidate might also question whether the ~$1M+ proceeds changes Nick's calculus about doing an MBA at all versus continuing to build the business
